kurz: Why a constant interest rate has an uneven effect, and why the term sits in the exponent of the compound interest formula.

bloecke.md:
Interest and compound interest differ only in what happens to the interest credited. If €100 is invested at 5% and the interest is withdrawn every year, the amount credited is always €5, for all fifty years. If the interest stays in the account instead, the credit is €5.25 in the second year, €7.76 in the tenth, €20.58 in the thirtieth and €54.61 in the fiftieth. In the fiftieth year alone, more than half of the capital originally invested is added.

The bank pays only the agreed interest throughout. The interest rate stays at 5% the whole time; what grows is the base to which it is applied. With [[Compound interest|compound interest]], the interest is therefore not paid out, it is added to the capital and earns interest itself the following year.

bloecke.erklaerung: i is entered as a decimal, so 5% as 0.05. n counts the compounding periods, which need not be years.

bloecke.md: The two calculations differ in the way repeated addition differs from repeated multiplication. With linear growth, the same amount is added in each period; with exponential growth, the total is multiplied by the same factor in each period. At first the difference is small. With €10,000 at 5%, the two curves are only €262.82 apart after five years, but €79,674 apart after fifty years.

bloecke.titel: €10,000 at 5% with and without reinvestment of interest
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Both lines are based on the same interest rate; for the upper line, the interest credited is added to the capital every year.

bloecke.md:
The most important property of the curve in practice is how growth is distributed over time, which cannot be read directly from the formula. Of the total growth that €10,000 generates over fifty years at 5%, 77% arises in the second half of the period. In the first 25 years, €23,863 of interest accumulates; in the second 25 years, €80,810.

A saver who stops after ten years therefore gives up the part of the growth that only arises late. Most of the compounding effect comes at the end of the term.

The interest rate determines the factor by which the capital grows each period. Time determines how often this factor is applied. Time sits in the **exponent**, the interest rate in the **base**. A longer term therefore usually has a greater effect than a higher interest rate.

bloecke.titel: Final value of €100 (lump-sum investment, annual compounding, excluding costs and taxes)

bloecke.md:
The table shows why differences of a few percentage points attract so much attention. Between 2% and 8%, the gap is €94 after ten years and €4,421 after fifty years. The three rates roughly correspond to the range of what different asset classes have delivered historically. The ECB's deposit facility rate, for example, has stood at 2.50% since 16 September 2026. As a net index in euros, the MSCI World returned 8.49% a year from 1988 to 2025, but only 6.26% over the shorter period from 2001 to 2025. The gap between 2% and 8% is therefore mainly due to higher risk and not to greater skill.

Despite these differences, the length of the investment has an even greater influence than the choice of interest rate, as a direct calculation shows.

punkte: Requires a different asset class and therefore more risk

bloecke.md: Doubling the term therefore yields slightly more than doubling the interest rate. It is also the only one of the two options that requires nothing but waiting. A longer investment period can also outweigh higher contributions. Two model savers each invest €200 a month at 6%. Anna pays in from age 25 to 40 and then leaves the portfolio untouched; Ben starts at 40 and pays in until 67. In total, Anna pays in €36,000 and Ben €64,800. At 67, Anna has around €292,700 and Ben around €161,300. Ben's additional contributions of €28,800 are not enough to make up for Anna's fifteen-year head start.

bloecke.titel: Short early savings plan and long late savings plan (€200 a month, 6% p.a.)
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with age on the x-axis. After the age of 40, Anna's curve keeps rising without further contributions, purely through interest on the existing balance.

bloecke.md:
Just under €4 a day adds up to around €120 a month. Over 40 years, €57,600 of your own money is paid into a securities account this way instead of being spent on coffee. This grows to:

- €111,127 at 3% p.a.
- €238,979 at 6% p.a.
- €418,921 at 8% p.a.

Illustrative calculation with monthly contributions paid at the end of each month and monthly compounding, excluding costs, taxes and inflation. The coffee is only an example. In general, a small amount over a very long period can achieve more than a large amount over a short one.

bloecke.titel: Savings plan with a €1,000 starting amount and €200 a month over 30 years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. The dashed line shows the €73,000 paid in, and the area above it shows interest and compound interest.

bloecke.md:
In this calculation, the same €73,000 of contributions grows to €100,366 at 2%, €170,919 at 5% and €309,008 at 8%. The share of the final value that comes from interest and not from the saver's contributions rises from 27% to 76%.

For a lump-sum investment, this share can be determined with a short formula. It is 1 − 1/(1+i)^n and depends only on the interest rate and the duration, not on the size of the amount. €500 gives the same share as €500,000.

bloecke.titel: Share of interest in the final value of a lump-sum investment
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using 1 − 1/(1+i)^n, as a percentage. From about 30 years and 6% upwards, more than four fifths of the wealth comes from returns and the rest from the amount paid in.

bloecke.md:
With debts, the same exponent works against the debtor as soon as the interest is added to the debt. This happens, for example, with an arranged overdraft, where the interest is charged to the account and then itself incurs interest. Default interest (Verzugszinsen) is different, because under Section 289 BGB (Civil Code) no further interest accrues on it. If a consumer is in default, an outstanding claim of €2,000 bears interest at five percentage points above the basic rate of interest (Basiszinssatz), that is, at 6.52% since 1 July 2026. After three years, it has thus grown to €2,391, and after ten years to €3,304. With compound interest, it would be €2,417 and €3,761.

Two other factors interrupt the compounding effect but are less noticeable. A withdrawal costs the final value that the amount withdrawn would have reached by the end of the term. Likewise, a euro deducted from the capital as a fee is not lost just once, because the interest it would have earned over the entire remaining term is lost with it.

n counts the compounding periods. If a nominal 5% is credited monthly, the calculation is (1 + 0.05/12)^12 = 1.051162. That corresponds to an effective 5.1162% a year. With daily crediting, it is 5.1267%. In the limiting case of arbitrarily frequent compounding, the factor tends towards Euler's number raised to the power of i, here e^0.05 = 1.051271, or 5.1271%.

At low interest rates, the gap between annual and continuous compounding is small, but it grows as the rate rises. At a nominal 20%, the effective rate is 21.94% with monthly compounding and 22.14% with continuous compounding. For this reason, German price indication law (Preisangabenrecht) requires the **annual percentage rate** to be stated for loans. It combines different compounding intervals and fee dates into a single comparable figure.

1. Compound interest requires reinvestment. A distributing fund whose distributions are credited to the current account and spent there generates no compound interest on that portion. With an accumulating fund, reinvestment happens automatically within the fund assets; with bond coupons and rental income, the investor has to arrange it themselves.
2. Equities have no fixed interest rate. A historical average such as the MSCI World's 8.49% since 1988 describes the past and is not a promise. The formula assumes a constant quantity that does not exist in reality. With real investments, the sequence of the years also matters.
3. The attribution to Einstein is not documented. The frequently quoted line about the eighth wonder of the world cannot be found in any verified source from his lifetime. The mathematical relationships hold regardless.

- Starting early matters more than optimising the investment. The first years bring little visible return but shift the entire curve to the left.
- The investment should not be interrupted, because a withdrawal costs the final value of the amount withdrawn.
- Reinvestment should happen automatically so that it does not have to be decided afresh every month.
- It makes sense to calculate with a cautious and an optimistic interest rate. What matters then is the range of outcomes, not the figure that looks best.

mitnehmen: With compound interest, ordinary interest is applied to capital to which the previous returns have been added.
Because time sits in the exponent and the interest rate only in the base, an extra decade usually has a greater effect than an extra percentage point.
Around three quarters of the growth arises in the second half of the period, so stopping early costs the most productive part.
Compound interest only arises if the returns are reinvested, so it depends on the investor's behaviour and not on the product.
With debts, fees and withdrawals, the same formula works against the debtor or investor.

begriffe.text: Interest on capital to which earlier interest credits have already been added. The final value is K × (1 + i)^n. Compound interest requires the returns to be reinvested.
Growth in which the stock is multiplied by a constant factor each period instead of a constant amount being added. A large part of the growth arises towards the end of the period.
Investing income received, such as interest, coupons or dividends, again. With accumulating funds, it happens automatically within the fund assets; otherwise the investor has to arrange it.
An annual interest rate that combines different compounding intervals and ancillary costs into one comparable figure. At a nominal 5% with monthly crediting, it is 5.1162%.

Reference rate calculated every six months under Section 247 BGB and published by the Deutsche Bundesbank. It has stood at 1.52% since 1 July 2026. Default interest for consumers is five percentage points above the basic rate of interest.
